**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: One Hour Forty Five Minutes.**

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES: Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
Read the extract below and answer the questions that follow:

**IS MORE GROWTH REALLY BETTER?**

> A number of writers have raised questions about the desirability of faster economic growth as an end in itself yet faster growth means more wealth and to most people the desirability of wealth is beyond question. I have been rich and I have been poor- and I can tell you "rich is better"; a noted stage personality is said to have an interview; and most people seem to have the same attitude about the economy as a whole. To those who hold this belief; a healthy economy is one that is capable of turning out vast quantities of shoes; food; cars and TV sets. An economy whose capacity to provide all these things is not expanding is said to have succumbed to the disease of stagnation....

*Source: ECONOMICS; Principles and Policy; Second Edition, by William Baumol and Alan S. Blinder; Pages 474-475.*

questions.enonce_markdown: Distinguish between potential economic growth and actual economic growth. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Actual economic growth** is the **increase in a country's real national output (real GDP) over a period of time**, usually a year, that is actually achieved. It is measured by the percentage change in real GDP (or real GDP per head) and it can be negative in a recession. It is shown by a movement from a point inside the production possibility curve towards the curve.

**Potential economic growth** is the **increase in the economy's productive capacity**, that is, the maximum output it could produce if all resources were fully and efficiently employed. It results from a larger quantity or better quality of resources or from better technology, and it is shown by an **outward shift of the production possibility curve** (or of the long-run aggregate supply curve).

**Difference:** actual growth is what the economy really produces; potential growth is what it could produce. An economy has actual growth without potential growth if it only uses idle resources (for example, falling unemployment), and it can have potential growth without actual growth when unemployed resources remain idle.

questions.enonce_markdown: Outline four reasons why economic growth is desirable. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four reasons why economic growth is desirable (1 mark each, with a short explanation):

1. **Higher living standards:** a larger real output per head means more goods and services (food, housing, consumer goods) for each person, which raises real income and welfare.
2. **Reduction of poverty:** a larger national income raises the incomes of the poor and gives the means to fight poverty and hunger.
3. **More employment:** growth increases the demand for labour and creates jobs, which reduces unemployment.
4. **Higher tax revenue and better public services:** the government can collect more taxes without raising tax rates and finance schools, hospitals, roads and other infrastructure.
5. **More resources for investment and development:** growth allows more saving and investment, which sustains further growth, and makes it easier to repay debt and to improve the balance of payments.
6. **Greater choice and national prestige:** a wider range of goods and a stronger position in the world economy.

Any four, outlined, earn full marks.

questions.enonce_markdown: List four disadvantages of economic growth. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four disadvantages of economic growth (1 mark each, any four):

1. **Environmental damage and depletion of resources:** more output and energy use lead to pollution, deforestation, loss of farmland and exhaustion of non-renewable resources such as oil.
2. **Widening inequality:** the gains of growth may go mainly to the rich or to certain regions or sectors, so the gap between rich and poor grows.
3. **Inflation and balance of payments pressure:** if demand grows faster than supply, prices rise, and extra income raises imports.
4. **Social costs (negative externalities):** congestion, noise, pollution, rapid urbanisation, rural depopulation, stress and loss of traditional culture.
5. **Opportunity cost:** to invest for growth, society must give up current consumption, so the present generation sacrifices some living standards.
6. **Structural unemployment:** new technology can make some skills obsolete and some workers redundant.

questions.enonce_markdown: When growth takes place a distinction is usually made between capital widening and capital deepening. Explain. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Both terms describe the way in which **capital accumulation** takes place when an economy grows.

**Capital widening** means that the capital stock increases **at the same rate as the labour force**, so that each new worker is equipped with the same amount of capital as existing workers. The **capital-labour ratio** (capital per worker) remains **unchanged**, so output rises, but output per worker (productivity) and income per head do not. For example, if the labour force rises by 5 per cent and the number of machines also rises by 5 per cent, there is only capital widening.

**Capital deepening** means that the capital stock increases **faster than the labour force**, so that the **capital-labour ratio rises**: each worker has more and better machinery. This raises **labour productivity** and therefore real output and income per head. It is the form of capital accumulation that leads to a lasting rise in living standards.

In short: widening provides capital for more workers; deepening provides more capital for each worker.

questions.enonce_markdown: Modern economic growth depends on a series of factors. Name four factors that can lead to a rapid rate of economic growth. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four factors that can lead to a rapid rate of economic growth (1 mark each, any four):

1. **Capital accumulation (a high rate of saving and investment)** in machinery, factories and infrastructure.
2. **Growth in the quantity and quality of labour:** a growing labour force, better education, training and health, which raise productivity (human capital).
3. **Technological progress and innovation:** new and better production methods raise output per worker.
4. **Natural resources:** discovery or better use of land, minerals, oil, forests and water.
5. **Entrepreneurship and a favourable business climate:** political stability, security of property rights, sound institutions and low corruption.
6. **Good infrastructure, openness to trade and stable macroeconomic policies** (transport, energy, export markets, low inflation).
